title: 24-hour pizza dough
subtitle: Slow-rise dough for Neapolitan and home-oven pizza
excerpt: A 24-hour cold-fermented pizza dough made with 00 flour, a little fast-action yeast, water, and salt. The long rest in the fridge builds flavour and gives the gluten time to relax, so the dough stretches easily and bakes with a blistered, lightly charred crust.
sourceNotes: Slow-fermented pizza dough is the Neapolitan tradition, codified by the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (1984) and widely disseminated through modern pizza writers including Ken Forkish, Flour Water Salt Yeast (2012), and Enzo Coccia, The Neapolitan Pizza (2012). The cold-fermentation method is the home-cook adaptation of the professional 1 to 3 day bulk ferment.

recipe.yieldDescription: 4 dough balls, each enough for one 30 cm pizza
recipe.freezeNotes: Dough balls freeze well after the first 24-hour ferment. Freeze individually in lightly oiled sealed bags. Thaw in the fridge overnight, then rest at room temperature for 2 hours before shaping.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles easily. Use the full kilo of flour for 8 dough balls.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make 24 to 48 hours ahead and keep in the fridge. Remove the dough balls 2 hours before shaping to let them come to room temperature.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process by which yeast consumes sugars in the flour and produces carbon dioxide, making the dough rise while also creating the compounds that give the finished crust its flavour.
The formation of elastic protein strands in dough through hydration and mixing; strong gluten lets you stretch the dough thin without it tearing.

content.text: This is a slow-fermented pizza dough made with 00 flour, a small amount of yeast, water, and salt. The 24-hour rest in the fridge does most of the work: the dough builds flavour through
fermentation
, the
gluten
relaxes, and by baking time it stretches to a thin disc without springing back. The finished crust blisters and chars at the edges and stays soft in the centre.

The recipe makes four balls. Bake what you need and freeze the rest. You can also keep the dough in the fridge for up to 48 hours, but beyond that the yeast runs out of food and the crust loses character.
What you need

items.prepNote: about half a standard 7 g sachet

content.text: Method
Mix the dough
Pour the water into a large bowl. Add the yeast and stir until dissolved.
Add the flour and mix with your hand or a spoon until no dry flour remains and a shaggy dough forms. Add the salt and mix again for 1 minute.
Turn the dough onto a clean surface and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. It should spring back slowly when poked.
First rest and divide
Oil a large bowl, place the dough inside, cover with cling film, and leave at room temperature for 1 hour. The dough will puff slightly.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and divide into 4 equal pieces, about 210 g each. Shape each piece into a tight ball by pulling the sides down and pinching them underneath.
Place each ball in a small oiled container or on a lightly oiled tray, cover with cling film, and refrigerate for 18 to 24 hours.
Before baking
Remove the dough balls from the fridge 2 hours before you plan to bake. Leave them covered at room temperature until they feel soft, slightly puffy, and no longer cold in the centre.

To shape: flour your hands and the surface lightly. Press the ball flat from the centre outward, leaving a 2 cm border untouched for the crust. Lift and stretch gently over your knuckles, rotating as you go, until the disc is about 30 cm across and even in thickness.

items.symptom: The dough tears when I stretch it
items.cause: Gluten is too tight, usually from insufficient rest at room temperature.
items.fix: Cover the dough and leave it for another 20 to 30 minutes. It will relax and stretch more easily.

items.symptom: The dough springs back and won't stay stretched
items.cause: Same cause as tearing: the gluten is tense and needs more rest.
items.fix: Leave it for 15 to 20 minutes, then try again. Cold dough always resists; warm, rested dough gives easily.

items.symptom: The dough smells sour or tastes sharp
items.cause: It has over-fermented, usually from being in the fridge longer than 48 hours or from too much yeast.
items.fix: Use it immediately; the crust will still be edible but slightly more acidic. Reduce the yeast to 1 g next time, or plan to use the dough within 24 hours.

items.symptom: The baked crust is pale and doughy in the middle
items.cause: Oven or pizza stone was not hot enough.
items.fix: Preheat your oven at its maximum setting for at least 45 minutes with a pizza stone or heavy tray inside. The stone needs to be scorching hot before the pizza goes on.

content.text: Where this dough comes from

The slow-fermented dough is the Neapolitan method, where pizza bakes in a wood-fired oven at 480°C for 60 to 90 seconds. At home, a very hot conventional oven with a heavy stone or steel gets close enough: the crust blisters, the cornicione (the rim) puffs, and the base stays thin and slightly chewy in the centre. The 24-hour ferment is the key difference from a same-day dough and the one thing worth building time around.
